(2020). 1.1.2 Cryogenic Hydrogen Hydrogen is a colorless, odorless gas and the lightest element on the periodic table at standard temperature and pressure (Royal Society of Chemistry n.d.). It is rarely found naturally in its pure, diatomic form (H ) on Earth but can be produced using energy-intensive chemical 2 processes. Instead, hydrogen is typically bonded to other elements such as oxygen and carbon, and found in water (H O), hydrocarbons, and other chemicals on Earth. While hydrogen has a 2 high gravimetric energy density (120 MJ/kg on a lower heating value basis), it has low volumetric mass density (0.09 kg/m3 at standard temperature and pressure) and must be compressed to 700 bar, or liquefied to −253°C (20 K), to achieve a volumetric energy density closer to other fuels (Figure 4). For aviation applications, fuels with high volumetric energy density are required such that the fuel does not take up considerable space on the aircraft. Therefore, limitations exist with using hydrogen as an energy source for aviation applications. Of the hydrogen options, liquefied (i.e., cryogenic) hydrogen (LH ) is the most viable and may be a 2 low-carbon energy solution for a select number of aircraft types and flight durations. 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Although methane is a major constituent of LNG, compositional variabilities are inevitable due to numerous feedstocks and sources for natural gas production and extraction. It may contain different hydrocarbon and non-hydrocarbon constituents, and compositions are never consistent. Consequently, important fuel properties relevant to aviation fuel screening may vary with feedstock and sources resulting in the potential need for a quality specification for LNG as an aviation fuel. Liquefication of natural gas drastically reduces volume requirements for storage; in the liquefied state, only 1/600th of the volume of the gaseous state is required (Raab et al. 2024). Despite its global availability, LNG has not been utilized in the aviation sector for commercial purposes due to the cryogenic nature of the fuel, fuel compositional variability, and changes in airport infrastructure required for large-scale adoption. However, it is extensively used in the marine sector and in automotive sector as LNG and compressed natural gas (American Bureau of Shipping 2022; DOE n.d.-c).
